## The puzzle

I follow a handful of South African banks on LinkedIn. The pitch, in my head, is reasonable enough: every now and then they post an interesting research note, or a graduate programme, or a job. Sometimes they even post a chart I want to steal.

The reality is that the most common thing those accounts produce in my feed is *other people* shouting at them. A customer can't get hold of a human, the chatbot is unhelpful, a UIF form has gone missing for two years — and so the customer tags the bank in a public post to make the problem expensive enough that someone notices.

Here is a fairly typical example I scrolled past this morning:

![A LinkedIn user pressing Old Mutual publicly about an unresolved HR/UIF issue. The reply ("thanks, please check your inbox") is the genre-defining response.](assets/Screenshot%202026-05-14%20at%2015.17.18.png)

I don't really care about Jackson's UIF forms. I'm sorry he's having a bad time, but seeing his post doesn't change my view of Old Mutual one way or the other. It just makes my feed slightly worse. I have unfollowed several banks for exactly this reason.

Here is what I want to understand. LinkedIn clearly *can* identify these posts — the boilerplate corporate reply ("Hi, thanks for raising this, please check your DMs") is a dead giveaway that the firm's social-media team has tooling for exactly this. So why does the algorithm keep pushing them into my feed? Why would it do something that annoys me, one of the very people it's trying to retain?

My answer: it annoys me now, but I'm staying on the platform *because* it might annoy someone else later on my behalf.

That is the whole argument. The model below just makes it precise.

## The split personality of a LinkedIn user

The thing about "a LinkedIn user" is that it's not a single type. It's one person in two possible states, with very different preferences in each:

- **Reader state**: I'm scrolling at 8am, I want research notes and job ads, and every grievance post is a minor tax on my attention. I would happily vote to suppress all of them.
- **Complainer state**: my UIF claim has been stuck for three months, nobody at the bank answers emails, and I need the public post to be seen by as many people as possible. I would happily vote to amplify all of them.

The same user, opposite preferences, depending on the day.

LinkedIn sets a single dial — call it $\alpha$, the probability that a given grievance post reaches users who follow the tagged company but not the poster — and that dial has to serve me in both states simultaneously. The platform cannot offer me "suppress everyone else's complaints but amplify mine." That's not how feeds work.

So LinkedIn is not, as I instinctively assumed, choosing between keeping complainers happy and keeping readers happy. It's choosing how much insurance to offer its users against their own future bad luck. The question is just whether that insurance premium — the annoying posts I see today — is worth paying.

## The model

### Setup

Two players: **User** ($U$) and **LinkedIn** ($L$). The user is in reader state with probability $1 - \pi$ in any given period and in complainer state with probability $\pi$. LinkedIn picks $\alpha \in [0, 1]$ once, and that choice applies in all periods.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\alpha$ | Platform's exposure parameter: fraction of grievance posts shown to followers of the tagged firm |
| $\pi$ | Per-period probability the user becomes a complainer |
| $g$ | Value of grievance resolution (what the user gains if their post leads to a fix) |
| $r$ | Probability a public post leads to resolution (higher $\alpha$ → higher $r$; I treat $r = r(\alpha)$, increasing) |
| $c$ | Cost to the user of seeing one irrelevant grievance post in reader state |
| $N$ | Expected number of grievance posts in the feed per period |
| $b$ | Per-period value of the useful content LinkedIn provides (research notes, jobs) |
| $\kappa$ | Quadratic cost to LinkedIn of high $\alpha$ (reader churn risk, viral blowup risk) |

### The user's expected payoff from $\alpha$

In reader state (probability $1 - \pi$), the user absorbs $N$ grievance posts and pays cost $c$ each:

$$U_\text{reader}(\alpha) = b - \alpha \cdot c \cdot N.$$

In complainer state (probability $\pi$), the user needs their post amplified and gets resolution probability $r(\alpha)$:

$$U_\text{complainer}(\alpha) = r(\alpha) \cdot g.$$

The user's expected per-period surplus is:

$$U(\alpha) = b + (1 - \pi)\bigl[-\alpha \cdot c \cdot N\bigr] + \pi \cdot r(\alpha) \cdot g. \tag{1}$$

For tractability I take $r(\alpha) = \alpha \cdot r_0$, where $r_0$ is the baseline resolution probability per unit of exposure. The user's payoff becomes linear in $\alpha$:

$$U(\alpha) = b - (1-\pi)\,\alpha\,c\,N + \pi\,\alpha\,r_0\,g. \tag{2}$$

The user strictly prefers $\alpha > 0$ if and only if the option value of future complaint amplification outweighs the current annoyance cost:

$$\pi\,r_0\,g \;>\; (1-\pi)\,c\,N. \tag{IC-U}$$

If this holds, the user would — from behind the veil of ignorance, not knowing which state they will be in — vote for $\alpha > 0$. If it fails, they would prefer a platform without grievance amplification at all.

### LinkedIn's problem

LinkedIn cares about retaining users and sells ads against their attention. Its objective is:

$$\max_{\alpha \in [0,1]} \;\; N_U \cdot U(\alpha) \;-\; \kappa\,\alpha^2, \tag{3}$$

subject to the user participation constraint $U(\alpha) \geq u_\text{outside}$, where $u_\text{outside}$ is the value of leaving the platform.

The $-\kappa\alpha^2$ term captures the non-linear costs of pushing $\alpha$ too high: a feed dominated by grievance posts drives away the marginal reader faster than linearly, and high-profile unresolved complaints occasionally go viral in ways that embarrass advertisers.

The first-order condition gives:

$$\alpha^\star = \frac{N_U \cdot A}{2\kappa}, \qquad A \equiv \pi\,r_0\,g - (1-\pi)\,c\,N. \tag{4}$$

The interior optimum is positive — LinkedIn wants some grievance posts in the feed — if and only if (IC-U) holds. In other words, **the platform amplifies complaints only when doing so is in the average user's own long-run interest.** The aligned incentives are not a coincidence; it is exactly why a user who grumbles about seeing Jackson's UIF complaint has not actually deleted their account.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)

theme_blog <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 10),
      legend.position  = "bottom",
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}

# --- baseline parameters ---
pi_val  <- 0.15   # 15 % chance of becoming a complainer in any given period
r0_val  <- 0.80   # resolution probability per unit alpha
g_val   <- 6      # grievance resolution value
c_val   <- 0.5    # annoyance cost per grievance post
N_val   <- 8      # expected grievance posts per period at alpha = 1
b_val   <- 3      # value of useful content (constant in alpha)
N_U     <- 1000
kappa   <- 400

A_val        <- pi_val * r0_val * g_val - (1 - pi_val) * c_val * N_val
alpha_star   <- max(0, min(1, N_U * A_val / (2 * kappa)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-user-payoff
#| fig-cap: "The user's alpha-dependent surplus (equation 2, net of b). The option value of future complaint resolution (slope π·r₀·g) is the upward pull; current annoyance cost (slope (1−π)·c·N) is the downward pull. At baseline parameters the option value wins narrowly and the user prefers α > 0. The dashed vertical marks LinkedIn's unconstrained optimum."
#| fig-height: 4

tibble(alpha = seq(0, 1, by = 0.005)) |>
  mutate(
    option_value   =  pi_val * r0_val * g_val * alpha,
    annoyance_cost = -(1 - pi_val) * c_val * N_val * alpha,
    net            =  option_value + annoyance_cost
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-alpha, names_to = "Component", values_to = "Value") |>
  mutate(Component = factor(Component,
    levels = c("option_value", "annoyance_cost", "net"),
    labels = c(
      paste0("Option value  (π·r₀·g = ", round(pi_val * r0_val * g_val, 2), ")"),
      paste0("Annoyance cost  ((1−π)·c·N = ", round((1-pi_val)*c_val*N_val, 2), ")"),
      "Net user surplus from α"
    )
  )) |>
  ggplot(aes(alpha, Value, colour = Component)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = alpha_star, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("label",
    x = alpha_star + 0.03, y = -1.5,
    label = paste0("α* = ", round(alpha_star, 2)),
    hjust = 0, size = 3, fill = "white", label.size = 0, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#4CAF50", "#E07B54", "#2196F3")) +
  labs(
    title    = "What does the user actually want?",
    subtitle = "Option value vs. annoyance cost; net surplus is positive when (IC-U) holds",
    x        = "Exposure parameter α",
    y        = "User surplus from α (relative to α = 0)",
    colour   = NULL
  ) +
  theme_blog()
```

### When does the user prefer $\alpha = 0$?

The condition (IC-U) can fail in two instructive ways:

1. **Low $\pi$**: if I almost never have an unresolved grievance, the insurance premium is never worth paying. A user who has robust private channels to firms — a relationship banker, a direct support contract — will rationally prefer $\alpha = 0$ and will find grievance posts genuinely annoying with no compensating benefit.

2. **High $N$**: if the feed is already flooded with grievances, the marginal annoyance cost $(1-\pi) c N$ rises while the option value stays constant. There is a threshold $N^\star = \pi r_0 g / [(1-\pi) c]$ above which even users who expect to complain occasionally would prefer less amplification.

These two cases are plotted below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ic-threshold
#| fig-cap: "Regions where (IC-U) holds and where it fails. Left panel: as π rises (user more likely to need the platform's enforcement), they tolerate higher N before preferring α = 0. Right panel: as N rises, the threshold π* rises — users need to expect complaints more often to justify the noisier feed."
#| fig-height: 4

# threshold N* as a function of pi
df_threshold <- tibble(pi = seq(0.01, 0.6, by = 0.005)) |>
  mutate(N_star = pi * r0_val * g_val / ((1 - pi) * c_val))

p1 <- ggplot(df_threshold, aes(pi, N_star)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#2196F3") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = N_val, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.55, y = N_val + 0.4,
    label = paste0("Baseline N = ", N_val), colour = "grey40", size = 3) +
  annotate("rect",
    xmin = 0, xmax = (1 - 1/(1 + r0_val * g_val / (c_val * N_val))),
    ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#E07B54", alpha = 0.07) +
  labs(
    title    = "Tolerance for grievance posts rises with π",
    subtitle = "Below the curve: prefer α = 0. Above: prefer α > 0.",
    x        = "π  (probability of needing the platform)",
    y        = "Maximum tolerable N*"
  ) +
  theme_blog()

# threshold pi* as a function of N
df_pi_thresh <- tibble(N = seq(1, 20, by = 0.1)) |>
  mutate(pi_star = c_val * N / (r0_val * g_val + c_val * N))

p2 <- ggplot(df_pi_thresh, aes(N, pi_star)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#E07B54") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = N_val, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = N_val + 0.3, y = 0.1,
    label = paste0("Baseline N = ", N_val), colour = "grey40", size = 3, hjust = 0) +
  labs(
    title    = "As feed gets noisier, users need higher π to stay",
    subtitle = "π* = threshold below which user prefers α = 0",
    x        = "N  (grievance posts per period at α = 1)",
    y        = "π* (minimum complaint probability to justify the feed)"
  ) +
  theme_blog()

library(patchwork)
p1 + p2
```

## Why the boilerplate reply still matters

The two-player model doesn't need firms explicitly, but it's worth noting why the boilerplate reply exists as a consequence of the mechanism above. If $\alpha^\star > 0$ and grievance posts routinely reach firm-followers, a firm that ignores them faces compounding reputational damage per unresponded post. The cheapest response is one that publicly signals "we have a process" — converting the grievance from a live accusation into an in-progress ticket — without actually committing to resolution. That is the "Hi, thanks for raising this, please check your inbox" template. It costs the firm one line of text and removes the reputational stakes. The actual resolution probability changes very little; the *visible* accusation disappears.

The reply is not aimed at Jackson. It is aimed at the audience. And the audience is me.

## A natural experiment: Google reviews in Germany

There is a useful comparison that pushes the mechanism the other way. In Germany, businesses can — and do — get negative Google reviews removed under defamation law after publication. [This Settle in Berlin write-up](https://www.settle-in-berlin.com/google-reviews-removal-defamation-in-germany/) walks through the mechanics.

In the model's terms, ex-post removal raises $p_\text{remove}$ — the probability a given negative post is litigated away before it accumulates enough views to force a response. The effective exposure a complainer can count on becomes $\tilde\alpha = \alpha \cdot (1 - p_\text{remove})$, which collapses toward zero when businesses litigate aggressively.

The prediction: (IC-U) fails for more and more users as $\tilde\alpha$ falls, because the option value $\pi \cdot r(\tilde\alpha) \cdot g$ shrinks. Google reviews in Germany become less informative — not because users stop being honest, but because the threat mechanism that would pressure firms into responding no longer works. The result is a platform with systematically fewer negative reviews that signals less information. Which is exactly the complaint you hear about German Google reviews.

LinkedIn in South Africa sits at the opposite corner. There is no equivalent legal pressure on grievance posts, $\alpha^\star > 0$ is LinkedIn's unconstrained choice, and the platform is keeping it there precisely because enough users are in the region where (IC-U) holds.

## Next steps

A few things this model simplifies away that would be worth adding:

- **Heterogeneous users.** I've treated all users as facing the same $\pi$. In practice, some users — freelancers, people in sectors with poor formal consumer protection — have much higher $\pi$ and will strongly prefer high $\alpha$. Others, with stable employment and direct firm access, will strongly prefer $\alpha = 0$. LinkedIn is implicitly catering to the median of this distribution, which skews the result.
- **Strategic complainers.** Once $\alpha^\star > 0$ is common knowledge, some people will post exaggerated or manufactured grievances to extract responses. The platform's optimal $\alpha^\star$ should be pushed down by this adverse selection, since each additional strategic post raises $N$ without raising the genuine option value.
- **Dynamics.** I've treated $\pi$ as exogenous. In reality, customer-service quality is itself a function of how much pressure the platform creates — if $\alpha^\star$ is high, firms invest more in customer service (to avoid the reputational cost), $g$ falls because fewer serious grievances arise, and $\alpha^\star$ adjusts downward. There may be a fixed point that is lower than the static model suggests.

I will probably keep unfollowing banks. But I'll keep the account.
